what: Global-E Online makes it possible for an online shop to sell abroad. It handles the parts that stop most retailers from selling internationally: showing local prices and currencies, calculating duties and taxes, arranging shipping and returns, and taking on the risk of the transaction.
customers: Online retailers and brands who want international customers without building the capability themselves, from large fashion houses to smaller direct-to-consumer brands. Shopify is both a major partner and a distribution channel.
money: Fees charged to merchants for the platform and services, as a percentage of cross-border sales.
Shipping, duties and related services, where Global-E passes much of the cost through.
moat: Cross-border e-commerce is a knot of problems — duties in hundreds of jurisdictions, local payment methods, currency, returns logistics, fraud — and solving it once for many merchants is far cheaper than each solving it alone. Global-E’s revenue grows automatically with its merchants’ international sales, and its partnership with Shopify puts it in front of a very large pool of exactly the right customers.
risks: The shares trade at about 39.9 times earnings and 25.8 times EV/EBITDA, which assumes growth continues at close to the current rate.
Much of the reported revenue is fulfilment cost passed through, so the headline figure overstates the economics: the service fee line is the real business.
The Shopify relationship is both the main growth channel and a dependency on a partner that could change terms or build competing capability.
Tariffs and changes to duty thresholds directly affect cross-border economics, and governments have been tightening them.
Thirteen analysts average a $50.92 target against a $35.10 price, a 45% gap indicating disagreement about the growth rate.
opportunities: Revenue has grown very fast, from $245.3M in 2021 to $962.2M in 2025, with trailing revenue of about $1.2B.
Free cash flow of $282.9M against a $5.9B market value is strong for a company still growing this quickly.
Cash of $320.0M against $23.5M of debt means growth is entirely self-funded.
Cross-border is still a small share of total e-commerce, so the market being addressed is far larger than the revenue achieved.
Revenue grows with merchants’ international sales without new sales effort, which is the most efficient kind of growth.
watch: Gross merchandise value through the platform and the take rate on it. Revenue includes pass-through shipping costs; the value of goods sold and the fee kept on them are what actually describe the business.
view: The first analytical job with Global-E is to separate the real revenue from the pass-through. A large share of what it reports is shipping and duties collected and paid on behalf of merchants — money that flows through rather than money earned. The business is the service fee on cross-border sales, and anyone valuing this on the headline revenue line is working with an inflated denominator. Look at gross merchandise value and the take rate instead.

What the company actually does is solve a problem that is genuinely hard and genuinely boring, which is the best combination. A fashion brand in Milan that wants to sell to a customer in Brazil faces duties it cannot calculate, a payment method it does not accept, a currency it does not price in, a shipping cost it cannot predict and a return it cannot process. Each of those is solvable and all of them together are why most retailers simply do not bother. Solving it once for thousands of merchants is enormously cheaper than each solving it alone, and that is a durable economic logic.

The Shopify relationship is the thing to think hardest about, because it is both the growth engine and the single point of failure. It puts Global-E in front of exactly the right merchants at the moment they decide to go international, which is why revenue went from $245 million to $962 million in four years. It also means a partner with its own ambitions controls the channel. Platform partnerships of this kind are a moat until the day the platform decides they are a margin opportunity.

At 39.9 times earnings you are paying for the growth to continue, and the honest external risk is policy rather than competition: governments have been tightening duty thresholds and raising tariffs, and the economics of a cheap cross-border parcel change materially when the duty-free allowance falls. That is outside anyone’s control and it affects the whole category. I would own this on the strength of the problem it solves and watch gross merchandise value, the take rate and the Shopify share of it — three numbers that between them tell you everything the income statement obscures.
bull: Cross-border stays a small, fast-growing slice of e-commerce, merchants keep adopting through Shopify, and the take rate holds as volume compounds.
bear: Tariff and duty-threshold changes make cheap cross-border parcels uneconomic while Shopify builds or buys the capability itself, and a 40 times multiple meets decelerating growth.
